title: Andhra Villagers Hold Frog Weddings to Pray for Rain as State Faces 48% Rainfall Deficit
excerpt: As El Niño squeezes India's 2026 monsoon to its weakest in 11 years, communities across Andhra Pradesh are reviving the centuries-old Mandooka Parinaya ritual, marrying frogs in elaborate ceremonies to invoke the rain god Varuna.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Andhra Pradesh faces a 48% rainfall deficit, prompting villagers to perform frog weddings for rain.
  • India's 2026 monsoon is expected to be the weakest in 11 years, at 90% of the long-period average.
  • The frog wedding ritual, known as Mandooka Parinaya, reflects deep agrarian dependence on monsoon rains.
  • Chief Minister Naidu urges sustainable water practices to combat recurring water shortages in the state.
  • 111 districts in India are classified as highly vulnerable due to low irrigation levels.

  • Villagers across Andhra Pradesh and neighbouring Telugu-speaking states are performing frog weddings — known locally as Kappala Pelli or Mandooka Parinaya — as the state records a 48% rainfall deficit this monsoon season.
  • Chief Minister N. Chandrababu Naidu has called on citizens to harvest rainwater and recharge groundwater to combat recurring water shortages.
  • India's 2026 monsoon is forecast at 90% of the long-period average, the weakest in 11 years, driven by a developing El Niño that threatens kharif crop yields across 315 vulnerable districts.
  • The frog wedding ritual, practised for centuries across at least seven Indian states, reflects deep agrarian dependence on monsoon rains and a folk belief that frog croaking summons Varuna, the rain god.

In parched villages across Andhra Pradesh, the soundtrack of desperation this July is not the usual monsoon patter on tin roofs but the rhythmic chanting of priests performing an ancient ceremony — one in which the bride and groom are both frogs.

As the state stares at a 48% rainfall deficit, farming communities have turned to Kappala Pelli, the Telugu name for the centuries-old frog wedding ritual, hoping to coax the rain god into breaking the dry spell that has cracked their fields and stalled kharif sowing.

A Ritual Rooted in Agrarian Faith

The practice, known formally as Mandooka Parinaya in Sanskrit, follows the template of a traditional Hindu wedding. Villagers catch a male and female frog — typically named Varuna (after the water god) and Varsha (meaning rain). The amphibians are bathed in turmeric paste, dressed in miniature wedding finery, and sometimes adorned with a mangalsutra and toe ring, mirroring the rituals of a human bride.

A priest performs the ceremony, chanting mantras while community members sing folk songs and beat drums. After the wedding, the newlywed frogs are released into a nearby pond or well, their croaking interpreted as a direct appeal to Indra and Varuna, the Vedic deities who govern rainfall.

"The croaking of frogs is like sweet music to the rain god's ears," goes the folk belief across states from Assam, where the ritual is called Bhekuli Biya, to Maharashtra and Karnataka, where similar ceremonies take place when the monsoon falters.

In Telangana's tribal Kolam community, the ritual takes an additional dimension: elders watch the direction in which a frog swims after being released into the village well, interpreting its movement as an indigenous weather forecast indicating which part of the village will receive the heaviest rains.

The 2026 Monsoon Crisis

This year's ceremonies carry more urgency than usual. India's monsoon rains have so far arrived about 43% below average, according to the India Meteorological Department, which has forecast an El Niño-weakened season that could deliver the lowest rainfall since 2015.

Andhra Pradesh is among the worst-hit states. Speaking at a Swachh Andhra event in Gudivada on July 18, Chief Minister N. Chandrababu Naidu confirmed the state's 48% rainfall deficit and urged citizens to adopt sustainable water practices, including rainwater harvesting and groundwater recharge.

Naidu recalled how declining inflows into the Krishna Delta had once devastated agriculture in the region known as India's "rice bowl" and pointed to the Pattiseema Lift Irrigation Project, which has diverted nearly 450 TMC of Godavari waters to the delta, as a buffer against reduced inflows this year.

The central government has classified 111 districts across India as highly vulnerable because less than a quarter of their farmland is irrigated. States including Andhra Pradesh have been directed to shift farmers toward less water-intensive crops such as pulses, millets, and oilseeds, according to Reuters.

Between Faith and Pragmatism

The frog wedding tradition has drawn a mix of reverence and scepticism. In 2019, when Udupi in Karnataka staged a widely covered frog wedding during a dry spell, meteorologists noted that the coincidental arrival of rain shortly after had no scientific connection to the ceremony. Environmental groups have occasionally objected to the practice on animal welfare grounds.

But for farmers who depend entirely on rain-fed agriculture — roughly 60% of India's farming population — the ritual is less about meteorology than about community resilience. The ceremonies bring villages together, offering a shared expression of hope during periods of acute anxiety over livelihoods.

Farm minister Shivraj Singh Chouhan told reporters in late June that the government would "not let farm fields remain empty" and confirmed that contingency plans, alternative crop advisories, and an El Niño Monitoring Cell were all in place.

For families in Andhra Pradesh's drought-prone interior, though, the question is more immediate: whether the rains will arrive in time to save seeds already sown in hardened, cracking soil. Until they do, the frogs will keep getting married.
